tests_declared: Dedicated axial T2 MRI of the cervical spine (C2 through C6)

resident.chief_complaint: Progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in the extremities for one year.
resident.history: A 63-year-old male presented with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in his extremities. He was graded Nurick grade 3 and modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score of 15. Cervical MRI showed severe cervical stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with associated hyperintense intramedullary signal change at C5-C6.
resident.physical_exam: Temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical examination notable for decreased cervical range of motion because of pain. The patient exhibited 5/5 strength in all muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities except for 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps. Sensation to light touch was decreased in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Bilateral upper and lower extremities revealed hyperreflexia.
key_positive_signs: 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps
Decreased sensation to light touch in bilateral upper and lower extremities
Bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia
Decreased cervical range of motion due to pain
resident.past_history: 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily and oxycodone 20 mg twice daily, remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001.
resident.public_message: This is a 63-year-old male with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic extremity pain (Nurick grade 3, mJOA 15). Cervical MRI demonstrated severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with T2 hyperintense signal change at C5-C6. Past medical history includes a 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg BID and oxycodone 20 mg BID, and remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001. Vital signs: temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical exam showed decreased cervical range of motion due to pain, 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps (otherwise 5/5), decreased light touch sensation bilaterally, and bilateral hyperreflexia. Hemoglobin 15 g/dL.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description of the imaging; the films were not available for review. The record describes severe cervical stenosis from C2-3 through C5-6, with associated hyperintense intramedullary cord signal change at C5-6. The direction of compression is not stated. These findings correlate highly with the reported progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical myelopathy, with the lesion most consistent with the cervical spinal cord at C5-C6 given the intramedullary signal change and bilateral upper extremity weakness plus hyperreflexia; the hyperreflexia in all four limbs localizes to the upper motor neuron pathways above C5.

red_flags.finding: Remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion (2001) with reported lower extremity symptoms.
red_flags.rationale: Does not explain the upper extremity hyperreflexia or weakness, and the lower extremity upper motor neuron signs are readily attributed to the cervical lesion; no evidence of active lumbar pathology is provided, so it does not change the indication or plan.

red_flags.finding: Neuropathic pain in all extremities and symmetric decreased light touch sensation, without a documented sensory level or peripheral nerve examination.
red_flags.rationale: These features could suggest a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but the presence of hyperreflexia and upper motor neuron signs indicates that cervical cord compression is the dominant cause of the myelopathic syndrome. This does not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis, though further electrodiagnostic testing could be considered if symptoms persist or confound assessment.

neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to the cervical spinal cord: bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia, bilateral biceps/triceps weakness, and gait difficulty are consistent with a cervical myelopathy, and the MRI findings of severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with cord signal change at C5-C6 explain the dominant syndrome (match level high). Two coexisting findings are noted: (1) the remote lumbar fusion does not alter the cervical localization or plan, and (2) the neuropathic pain and symmetric sensory loss raise the possibility of a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but they do not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis because hyperreflexia indicates central nervous system involvement.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk: moderate. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no formal airway assessment is recorded. Prone position tolerance: moderate.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3 months of structured conservative management, with reassessment every 6 weeks
preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of myelopathic signs: decline in mJOA score by 2 or more points, new bowel or bladder dysfunction, or new motor weakness
Progression of gait impairment or falls
New or worsening cervical cord signal change on follow-up MRI
Intractable neuropathic pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Failure to show stabilization or improvement by 3 months
physiatrist_opening.public_message: While severe cervical stenosis with cord signal change and progressive myelopathy is concerning, I propose a time-limited trial of structured conservative management before surgery. The patient's deficits, though significant, have not shown acute deterioration, and surgery carries non-negligible risk given his poorly controlled hypertension and smoking history. A 3-month program of physical therapy, pain management, strict activity modification, and close monitoring is a reasonable first step. I estimate the conservative success rate in this specific presentation at approximately 10%—low but not zero—and therefore I cannot yet concede that surgery is the only option. The preconditions for declaring conservative failure are explicit: any worsening of myelopathic signs, new gait or balance decline, or intractable pain would trigger immediate surgical referral. Until those criteria are met, I maintain my stance for conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Director points again to the cord signal change at C5-C6 and the progressive myelopathy, and states a 10% success rate is too low when irreversible cord injury is possible. I have already weighed those exact findings: I acknowledged the cord signal change and progressive myelopathy in my initial assessment, and I set a strict 3-month trial with immediate surgical referral on any worsening. The Director adds no new finding; the statement that a 10% success rate is too low is a risk-tolerance judgment, not evidence. Furthermore, the Director himself has determined that further imaging is necessary before surgery can proceed, which means there is currently no immediate surgical plan; that interval can be used to start conservative care without additional delay. Unless a specific finding is identified that shows my 3-month monitored trial poses an unacceptable incremental risk compared with the inherent delay of obtaining and interpreting new imaging, I maintain my stance for conservative care.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 63-year-old man has progressive cervical myelopathy (Nurick 3, mJOA 15) with severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 and T2 cord signal change at C5-C6. The clinical and imaging findings are concordant and indicate the need for decompression to prevent further irreversible cord injury. A conservative trial, as proposed by physiatry, carries only a 10% success rate and risks allowing neurologic decline while waiting for the predefined failure criteria. I recommend surgical decompression now.
proposed_options: Posterior C2-C6 decompressive laminectomy with C2-C6 instrumented fusion
C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome laminectomy (if C2 compression can be adequately addressed without fusion)
Continued conservative management for 3 months with close monitoring (not recommended as primary management)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior C2-C6 decompressive laminectomy with C2-C6 instrumented fusion
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's recommendation for a 3-month conservative trial: progressive myelopathy with cord signal change is a surgical indication, and waiting risks irreversible neurologic decline despite the 10% stated success.

The direction of compression is not stated in the imaging record. I would not finalize the surgical approach without reviewing the actual films or obtaining additional imaging to confirm whether the compression is predominantly anterior, posterior, or circumferential, as this determines whether an anterior, posterior, or combined approach is needed.

The need to include C2 in the decompression and fusion is unsettled; some may argue for C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome, but I would include C2 to fully decompress the C2-C3 stenosis and stabilize with fusion.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree with proceeding to surgery now rather than a conservative trial, and if so, with what urgency (elective vs urgent)?
Given the severe C2-C3 stenosis, do you favor extending decompression and fusion to include C2, or would you consider a C2 dome with C3-C6 laminoplasty after reviewing the imaging?
Should we obtain a CT myelogram or dedicated MRI sequences (e.g., axial T2 at each level) to clarify the principal direction of compression before finalizing the construct?
vice_opinions.public_message: My assessment is progressive cervical myelopathy with severe C2-C6 stenosis and cord signal change at C5-C6; surgical decompression is indicated. I prefer posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion, but I need to review the imaging to confirm the direction of compression. I disagree with a conservative trial: a 10% success rate is not enough when irreversible cord injury is possible. I have open questions: should we include C2 in the construct, and should we obtain additional imaging before finalizing? I look to you for the final decision.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 63-year-old man with progressive cervical myelopathy (Nurick 3, mJOA 15), severe C2-C6 stenosis, and T2 cord signal change at C5-C6. Surgical decompression is indicated to prevent irreversible cord injury; a monitored conservative trial is not acceptable given the low 10% success rate and the risk of further deterioration. The exact surgical approach depends on the compression vector and degree of C2-C3 involvement, which is why the CT myelogram and axial T2 sequences are necessary.
proposed_options: If imaging shows predominantly anterior compression: anterior cervical discectomy/corpectomy and fusion from C3 to C6, extending to C2-C6 if C2-C3 stenosis is significant.
If imaging shows posterior or circumferential compression: posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion, including C2 in the fusion construct if C2-C3 is involved.

If axial imaging shows adequate space at C2-C3 without significant cord compression: C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome may be considered, but I would still favor fusion over laminoplasty because of the long segment and risk of post-laminectomy kyphosis.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion, contingent on imaging showing posterior or circumferential compression; I would include C2 in the fusion if C2-C3 stenosis is significant rather than rely on a C2 dome.
disagreement_points: I continue to disagree with a conservative trial: the physiatrist's 3-month monitored delay carries an unacceptable risk of irreversible cord injury when the success rate is only 10%.
The choice between anterior and posterior remains unsettled until imaging shows the compression vector; committing to one approach before that would be premature.

Whether C2 must be included in the construct is contested: if C2-C3 stenosis is severe, a C2 dome laminoplasty may be insufficient. I lean toward including C2 in a fusion construct for a more reliable decompression and to prevent late kyphosis, but this needs the imaging to confirm.
deferred_questions_to_director: After the CT myelogram and axial T2 are reviewed, do you want the final surgical approach decided in this meeting, or will you decide after the radiologist and neurologist report?

If imaging shows anterior compression with significant C2-C3 involvement, would you consider an anterior C2 corpectomy, or do you prefer to rely on a posterior indirect decompression? I need your guidance on how aggressive to be at C2-C3.
Should I provisionally book the operating room and instrumentation for either anterior or posterior based on your contingency plan, or wait until the imaging review?
vice_opinions.public_message: I agree that surgery is indicated and that we must first clarify the compression vector and C2-C3 involvement. My preference remains posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion if the compression is posterior or circumferential, and I would include C2 in the fusion if C2-C3 stenosis is significant. I continue to oppose any conservative delay. I have open questions for you: whether to provisionally book the OR before imaging, and whether the final approach should be settled in our next meeting after the new studies are reviewed.

delegated_tasks: Chief Resident: obtain a detailed interval history of symptom progression over the last month, specifically any new weakness, falls, or bowel/bladder symptoms; document current mJOA score.

Radiologist: retrieve and review the original cervical MRI, and after the ordered axial T2 and CT myelogram are completed, report the predominant direction of compression (anterior, posterior, circumferential) at each level from C2-C3 to C5-C6, with special attention to C2-C3.

Neurologist: provide a written opinion on whether any clinical features suggest a more urgent timeline than elective, and whether the coexisting sensory symptoms alter the risk of waiting for imaging.

director_rulings.public_message: I have heard the competing views and the deputy director's open questions. As things stand, I believe surgery is indicated: this is a progressive cervical myelopathy with cord signal change at C5-C6 and severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6. The physiatrist's conservative trial is thoughtfully framed with explicit failure criteria, but a 10% success rate is too low when irreversible cord injury is possible; I cannot endorse a 3-month delay. At the same time, I cannot finalize the surgical approach without clarifying the direction of compression and the degree of C2-C3 involvement. Therefore I am ordering a CT myelogram and dedicated axial T2 sequences. I ask the Chief Resident to confirm the exact progression timeline and any new deficits, the radiologist to retrieve and review the original films and then interpret the new imaging with specific attention to the compression vector, and the neurologist to comment on the urgency of intervention. We will reconvene when these results are available. My contingency plan is as follows: if imaging shows predominantly anterior compression, we will plan an anterior decompression approach; if predominantly posterior or circumferential, a posterior C2-C6 decompression with fusion including C2 if needed; if axial imaging demonstrates adequate space at C2-C3 with no significant cord compression there, a C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome may be considered.

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated. I reject the physiatrist's request for a 3-month conservative trial: a 10% success rate is too low when progressive myelopathy and C5-C6 cord signal change carry a risk of irreversible injury, and the delay for imaging does not justify that risk. The surgical approach will be finalized after review of the CT myelogram and axial T2, but the operation is authorized now. If imaging shows predominantly anterior compression, we proceed with an anterior decompression. If posterior or circumferential, we proceed with posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion, including C2 in the fusion if C2-C3 stenosis is significant. If axial imaging shows adequate space at C2-C3 with no significant cord compression there, a C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome may be considered.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Decompression surgery with approach determined by pending imaging: anterior decompression if predominantly anterior compression; otherwise posterior C2-C6 laminectomy with instrumented fusion (include C2 if C2-C3 stenosis is significant) or C3-C6 laminoplasty with C2 dome if C2-C3 is adequately decompressed.
